passages.t: Two smoldering stubs, and Stand firm in faith
passages.happening:
In the days of King Ahaz, Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel march against Jerusalem, but they cannot overpower it (verse 1). When the news reaches the house of David, ‘the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind’ (verse 2).

The LORD sends Isaiah with his son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field (verse 3). He is to tell the king, ‘Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood’ (verse 4). The two kings have plotted to invade Judah and set up the son of Tabeal as king (verses 5-6). ‘It will not arise; it will not happen’ (verse 7).

The head of Aram is Damascus and its head is Rezin; the head of Ephraim is Samaria and its head is the son of Remaliah (verses 8-9). ‘If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The setting is the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 to 732 BC. Rezin, ruling from Damascus, and Pekah, ruling from Samaria, were organizing resistance to Assyria and tried to force Judah to join. When Ahaz refused, they invaded to replace him with a puppet. The books of Kings and Chronicles tell the same story. Against Isaiah's counsel, Ahaz sent silver and gold from the temple to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria and asked him for help. Assyria's own records list Jehoahaz of Judah, the full form of Ahaz's name, among the kings who brought tribute.

Isaiah meets the king at the water supply, probably because Ahaz was inspecting it in preparation for a siege. He brings his son, whose name Shear-jashub means a remnant will return, a walking message of both threat and promise.

The argument of verses 8 and 9 is built on a pattern. The heads of Aram and Ephraim are named. The head of Judah is left for Ahaz to supply: the LORD. The last line is a wordplay in Hebrew, roughly if you will not be firm in faith, you will not be made firm at all. The same meeting place returns in chapter 36, where Hezekiah, Ahaz's son, will do what Ahaz refused to do.
passages.later: Kings records what Ahaz did instead: he sent to Assyria saying, ‘I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me’ (2 Kings 16:7). A generation later the Assyrian envoy ‘stopped by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field’ (Isaiah 36:2). And King Jehoshaphat had once told his people, ‘Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld’ (2 Chronicles 20:20).
passages.asks: Ahaz's heart shook like trees in the wind, and God called his enemies two smoldering stubs. Ask what threat in your life looks huge to you and small to God. And ask what it would mean for you to stand firm in faith rather than run to the nearest strong ally.

passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Ahaz again: ask for a sign, ‘whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven’ (verse 11). Ahaz answers, ‘I will not ask; I will not test the LORD’ (verse 12).

Isaiah says, ‘Hear now, O house of David’ (verse 13). Is it not enough to try the patience of people, without trying the patience of God as well?

‘Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel’ (verse 14). He will eat curds and honey by the time he knows to reject evil and choose good (verse 15). ‘For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste’ (verse 16).

But the LORD will bring on Ahaz and his house a time unlike any since Ephraim split from Judah. He will bring the king of Assyria (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Kings in the ancient world consulted their gods before war, and Assyrian kings kept diviners to read omens. Israel was forbidden divination, but the LORD sometimes gave a sign to confirm his word, to Moses, to Gideon and later to Hezekiah. So the offer of a sign was extraordinary but not strange. Ahaz's refusal borrows the pious language of Deuteronomy, do not test the LORD, but he had already decided to trust Assyria.

Isaiah turns from Ahaz to the house of David. The you of verses 13 and 14 is plural. The sign is given to David's royal house as a whole.

Immanuel means, as Matthew explains it, ‘God with us’ (Matthew 1:23). Curds and honey were the food of a land returned to pasture, where fields had gone wild. Before the child was old enough to choose right from wrong, the threat from Aram and Israel would be gone. That part of the prophecy was fulfilled quickly: Damascus fell in 732 BC and Rezin was executed, Galilee and Gilead were taken the same year, and Samaria fell in 722 BC.

The king Ahaz ran to would become the next danger. The Assyrian flood came under Sennacherib in 701 BC.
passages.later: Matthew writes of Jesus' birth: ‘All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet’ (Matthew 1:22), and quotes the Greek of this verse: ‘Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel’ (Matthew 1:23). The name returns in Isaiah's next chapter: ‘its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel’ (Isaiah 8:8).
passages.hard:
Does Isaiah 7:14 predict a virgin birth, or was it a sign for Ahaz's own day?

The question is old and serious, and these notes set out the readings in their own terms. The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age. The word for a virgin in the strict sense is betulah. The verse ties the sign to a timetable of a few years: before the boy can tell good from evil, the lands of the two kings will be deserted, which happened by 732 BC. On this reading the sign concerned a child born then, perhaps in the king's household or to Isaiah. Trypho, in Justin Martyr's dialogue, applied the verse to Hezekiah. Rashi applied it to Isaiah's wife and son. Modern Jewish scholarship and many Christian critical scholars, such as Raymond Brown, agree that Isaiah spoke of a child of his own time, and Jewish readers add that Matthew's argument depends on the Greek word rather than the Hebrew.

Christian answers fall into three groups. Some, such as E. J. Young and J. Alec Motyer, read the verse as a direct prophecy of the Messiah's virginal conception. They point to the definite article (the almah), to the solemn offer of a sign as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven, and to the titles the same child receives in 8:8 and 9:6, which no ordinary child could bear. A second group holds a double fulfillment: a child born in Ahaz's day was the immediate sign, while the name Immanuel and the growing portrait of chapters 8 to 11 pointed beyond him to Jesus. A third stresses how Matthew uses fulfillment elsewhere, as when he applies Hosea 11:1 to Jesus' return from Egypt: he sees in Jesus the completion of a pattern, not only the answer to a single prediction.

On the translation question, the Greek word parthenos was chosen by Jewish translators before Christianity existed, so the rendering cannot be blamed on Christian bias. On every Christian reading, the church's confession of Jesus' virginal conception rests on the Gospel accounts in Matthew and Luke, not on the Hebrew word alone. How directly Isaiah foresaw it is a question on which faithful interpreters still differ.
passages.asks: Ahaz refused a sign because he had already chosen what to trust. Ask whether your caution is sometimes a cover for unbelief. And ask what it means to you that the sign God gave a faithless king was named Immanuel, God present with his people.

passages.t: Flies, bees, and a hired razor
passages.happening:
Four short oracles follow, each beginning on that day. ‘On that day the LORD will whistle to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in the land of Assyria’ (verse 18). They will settle in every ravine and thornbush (verse 19).

‘On that day the Lord will use a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates’ (verse 20), the king of Assyria, to shave the head, the legs and the beard.

On that day a man will keep a young cow and two sheep, and all who remain will eat curds and honey (verses 21-22). And where a thousand vines once stood, worth a thousand shekels of silver, ‘only briers and thorns will be found’ (verse 23). Men will go there with bow and arrow, and the tilled hills will become grazing for oxen and sheep (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Egypt and Assyria were the two great powers on either side of Judah. God whistles for them as a beekeeper calls his bees. The first hearers were told that the empires they feared and courted came and went at God's call.

The razor hired from beyond the Euphrates is a sharp irony. Ahaz had paid Assyria to save him. God says Assyria will be his hired razor, used on Judah. Shaving the head and beard was a deep humiliation in the ancient world, done to captives and mourners.

The curds and honey of verses 21 and 22 are the food of a ruined land. With the fields gone wild, a few animals give more milk than the few survivors can drink. The vineyards worth a fortune become thornbushes where men hunt.
passages.later: Chronicles records the cost of Ahaz's choice: the Assyrian king ‘came to Ahaz but afflicted him rather than strengthening him’ (2 Chronicles 28:20). And Isaiah later calls Assyria ‘the rod of My anger’ (Isaiah 10:5).
passages.asks: Ahaz paid Assyria to save him, and Assyria became the razor. Ask what you are paying for safety that may turn against you. And ask where you have trusted a strong helper more than God.
